exp.1:16:
They say that the words of those false teachers spread like gangrene, a disease that destroys healthy tissue little by little. The word "eat" in the verse means that it gnaws away or consumes. Hymeneus and Philetus are two concrete examples of those who did this.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, from prison, near the end of his life. He wants Timothy to guard sound teaching. These men were saying that the resurrection had already happened, and in this way they were unsettling the faith of some. Paul names them so that Timothy knows the danger is real.

For today: not everything that sounds spiritual is healthy. Measure what you hear against the Bible, and avoid empty talk that gradually draws people away from the gospel, even when it seems harmless.
exp.2:4:
He says there are people who look very religious on the outside but reject the power of God that transforms a life. "Form of godliness" is an image of devotion. "Power" is the word for effective force. "Turn away" means: keep away from them, do not let their example pull you along.

The apostle Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, from prison, near the end of his life. He has just described what people will be like in the last days: selfish, lovers of pleasure rather than of God. He wants to warn Timothy about the dangers inside and around the church, so that he will guard his faith and his ministry.

For today: it is not enough to attend church or speak well of God. Ask yourself honestly whether your faith is changing your character, the way you treat others, and your decisions. And be careful about who you spend time with, so that others do not put out your faith.
exp.0:0:
Paul introduces himself as an apostle, that is, a messenger sent by Jesus Christ. He says he is one "by the will of God," meaning that God called him and he did not choose the role himself. He also says that his mission is tied to the promise of life found in Christ Jesus: a true and eternal life that God offers through his Son.

Paul writes this letter to Timothy, his young co-worker and beloved son in the faith. According to Christian tradition, he writes while imprisoned, near the end of his life, although the exact details are debated. He begins with his identity and his calling in order to encourage and strengthen Timothy.

Today, this verse reminds us that our lives have meaning because God called us and gave us the promise of life in Christ. When you feel tired or unsure, remember that your service rests on God's promise, not on your own strength.
exp.2:5:
They are the ones who sneak into homes and take advantage of weak-willed women. The source uses a diminutive that describes their spiritual fragility at that time, and that comparison needs no separate word here. Those women were weighed down by guilt and ruled by desires that were out of control, and they were held captive, meaning they were trapped and manipulated as these men pleased.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, from prison, near the end of his life. He warns him about people who look religious but whose lives have not been changed. His purpose is for Timothy to recognize them and stay away from them. Paul is speaking about one specific group of deceivers, not about all women.

For today: do not be swayed by someone who sounds very spiritual. Compare what they teach and how they live with the Bible, and seek forgiveness and freedom in Christ, not in people who control you.
exp.1:14:
This verse encourages us to make a serious effort to live in a way that God approves. It speaks of a workman who has nothing to be ashamed of because he does his work well. "Rightly dividing" means "teaching or handling accurately and uprightly." "The word of truth" is God's message.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, from a difficult moment in his life. Earlier he spoke of God's faithfulness and warned against arguments over words that harm those who listen. Then he mentions Hymenaeus and Philetus, who were teaching falsehoods. Paul contrasts the faithful workman with those who get tangled up in empty talk.

For today: set aside regular time to read the Bible carefully, in its context, and ask God to help you understand it and live it. In this way you will speak with humility and truth, without seeking to win arguments.
exp.3:0:
Paul tells Timothy that he is giving him a solemn charge, as if before a court. Paul gives this charge in the presence of God and of Jesus Christ, who will judge the living and the dead when he appears (when he returns) and establishes his kingdom.

Paul is writing from prison, near the end of his life, to Timothy, his young co-worker who was pastoring in Ephesus. He knows he will soon depart, and so he entrusts him with the task of preaching the Word faithfully, even when many do not want to hear sound teaching.

For today: live and serve knowing that Christ sees everything and will one day call us to account. This should not produce fear, but seriousness and hope. Today, be faithful in what God has entrusted to you, without seeking the applause of people.
exp.3:9:
For Demas left Paul alone because he loved "this present world," that is, this world and its comforts. He went to Thessalonica. The passage also mentions that Crescens went to Galatia and Titus to Dalmatia. "Left alone" means abandoned, and "soon" means quickly.

Paul writes from prison, near the end of his life, to his young co-worker Timothy. He wants Timothy to come soon. Demas had been with Paul before (Colossians 4:14). It is not known for certain whether Crescens and Titus left on Paul's assignment or for some other reason; the text does not criticize them as it criticizes Demas.

Loving the things of this world can slowly cool our commitment to Christ. Today we can ask ourselves what things compete for our hearts. We can also accompany and encourage those who serve in the midst of hardship, as Paul needed faithful companionship.
exp.1:9:
He says Paul endures every suffering for the sake of "the elect," that is, those whom God calls to believe. His desire is that they also obtain "the salvation" that comes through Jesus Christ, together with the glory that lasts forever.

Paul writes this letter to his young co-worker Timothy while he is in prison, treated like a criminal. Even so, he remembers that the word of God is not chained. His suffering does not discourage him, because he sees that it serves so that others may come to know Christ. Then he quotes a faithful saying about suffering and reigning with Christ.

For today: when something costs you, such as an injustice, weariness, or mockery for your faith, ask God how He can use that to bless others. Your perseverance can encourage someone else to trust in Christ.
exp.1:18:
Even though some people wander away from the truth, what God has established does not waver. That foundation has, as it were, a seal, a mark of ownership, with two statements: the Lord knows those who are his, and everyone who claims the name of Christ must depart from iniquity. Iniquity means injustice or wickedness.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, from a difficult moment. He has just mentioned Hymenaeus and Philetus, who taught errors and confused some believers. Paul wants to encourage Timothy: false teaching unsettles people, but God's work stands firm. The two statements of the seal seem to recall passages from the Old Testament, such as Numbers 16, although some scholars interpret them in other ways.

For today: when you see confusion or failure in the church, rest in the fact that God knows those who are his. And examine your own life: if you bear the name of Christ, ask him for help to leave behind what does not please him.
exp.1:7:
He says that Timothy must remember Jesus Christ, a descendant of King David, who was raised from the dead. This is part of the gospel that Paul preaches. The word "seed" means descendants, and the phrase "according to my gospel" means according to the message that Paul proclaims.

Paul writes to Timothy from prison, near the end of his life. He encourages him to remain faithful in ministry, even though suffering may come. After speaking about the effort of the farmer, he points to Jesus as the center of everything. Being a descendant of David shows that he fulfills God's promises, and the resurrection shows his victory.

For today: when you feel tired or discouraged, do not look first at your problems, but at Jesus alive. Take a moment each day to remember that He rose again, and ask Him for strength to keep going.
exp.1:10:
This verse says that it is a trustworthy and reliable teaching: if we have died with Christ, we will also live with him. "Faithful saying" means a message you can trust completely. "Dead with him" is understood in several ways: joining Christ in his death through baptism and faith, or being willing to die for him if it is required.

Paul writes to Timothy from prison, and he says he suffers for the sake of the chosen ones, so that they may attain salvation. He seems to be quoting a saying well known among believers to encourage Timothy to persevere. The verses that follow speak of reigning with Christ, of denying him, and of his faithfulness.

For today: when following Jesus costs you something, such as giving up something or enduring mockery, remember that it is not in vain. Hand him a difficult decision today and trust that his promise of life is firm.
exp.0:1:
Paul greets Timothy by calling him "my dearly beloved son," an expression of spiritual affection, not necessarily of blood relation. He wishes him three things from God the Father and from Christ Jesus: grace (the favor we do not deserve), mercy (compassion that forgives and helps), and peace (well-being and tranquility that come from being right with God). The phrase "our Lord" acknowledges Jesus as the one who rules over the life of both of them.

Paul writes this letter from prison, toward the end of his life, according to the most common Christian tradition. Timothy was his close co-worker and a young man in the ministry. Paul encourages him to remain firm and without fear. That is why he begins with tenderness, before giving instructions and warnings.

For today: when you encourage someone who is tired or afraid, begin with affection and a sincere blessing. You might pray for that person or write them a few words asking God for them the grace, mercy, and peace of God.
exp.0:8:
He says that God saved us and called us with a holy calling, that is, to live set apart for him. This was not because of what we had done, but because of his own purpose and grace (the word "purpose" is the meaning of the original term). That grace was given to us in Christ Jesus before the world began, that is, from before time itself began. Salvation springs from God's plan and love, not from our merits.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, from prison. Timothy seemed to be afraid and ashamed because of the gospel and because of Paul's suffering. So Paul reminds him that his strength does not come from himself, but from the power of God and the grace he has received.

For today: when you feel unworthy or afraid to speak of your faith, remember that your worth does not depend on your performance. Rest in God's grace and serve him with confidence and gratitude.
exp.2:10:
Paul reminds Timothy of the persecutions and afflictions he himself suffered in the cities of Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra. He says that he endured them, and that the Lord delivered him from all of them. "Came upon me" means that they happened to him, that they fell on him.

Paul writes this letter to Timothy, his disciple, from a difficult moment, probably near the end of his life. Those three cities appear in the book of Acts (chapters 13 and 14), where Paul was persecuted and stoned in Lystra. Timothy was from that region, so he knew that story well. Paul encourages him to follow his example.

For today: if you follow Christ, there will be moments of difficulty. Remember how God has sustained you before, and let that give you confidence to remain steadfast today.
exp.1:20:
If a person turns away from what is wrong, he will be like a clean vessel set apart for a good purpose. He will be "precious", that is, valuable in God's eyes; "holy", meaning dedicated to him; and "useful" to the Lord. "Prepared" means made ready and equipped for every good work.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, from a difficult time. There were false teachers in the church who caused arguments and confusion. Paul uses the image of a large house with vessels of different materials. Interpreters explain "these things" from which one must cleanse oneself in various ways, but the context points to wickedness and the errors that were harming the church.

For today: God does not look for perfect people, but for available ones. Ask him to show you something you should leave behind, such as a habit, a harmful friendship or a useless argument, and let it go, so that he may use you.
exp.2:9:
Paul tells Timothy that he knows him well and has followed his life closely. "Doctrine" is what Paul taught; "manner of life" is the way he lived; "purpose" is his aim or goal; "longsuffering" is patience with people; "charity" is love; and "patience" is endurance through trials.

Paul writes from prison, near the end of his life, to his young companion Timothy. Earlier he spoke of false teachers who oppose the truth. Now he sets them against his own example, which Timothy saw up close. Soon he will remind Timothy of the persecutions Paul endured and how the Lord delivered him.

For today: faith is caught more through example than through words. Think of someone whose life matches what they believe, and learn from their steadfastness. And make sure that your own way of living, with love and patience, is also a good example for others.
exp.1:23:
This verse says that the servant of the Lord must not be quarrelsome, meaning someone who fights or argues about everything. Rather, he must be gentle and kind with everyone, able to teach clearly, and patient when people treat him badly or fail to understand him.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker who was caring for the church. Earlier he had warned him to avoid foolish arguments, because they only produce fights. Then he explains that correction must be given with gentleness, in the hope that God will lead those who oppose the truth to repent and come to know it.

For today: when someone thinks differently from you about your faith, do not aim to win the argument. Listen, respond calmly, and explain with patience. Often the tone opens a heart more than the arguments do.
exp.1:11:
It says that those who endure suffering for following Christ will also reign with him. But those who deny him, that is, reject him or give him up, will be denied by him. The word "deny" in the verse is an older form of the word "deny" used here, so no separate explanation is needed.

Paul writes to Timothy from prison, near the end of his life. He has just said that he endures everything for the sake of the chosen ones. He quotes a faithful saying, probably a well-known saying among believers, to encourage Timothy not to be ashamed of the gospel. Scholars debate whether "deny" here describes a complete renunciation or also temporary failures. The next verse shows that Christ remains faithful.

Today, when being faithful to Jesus costs you something, such as mockery, loss, or discomfort, remember that this steadfastness is not lost. Ask God for strength not to hide your faith, and trust that he sustains you.
exp.0:5:
Paul tells Timothy to stir up the gift of God, that is, to rekindle it the way a fire that is dying is fanned back to life. That gift came from God and was received when Paul laid his hands on him, a gesture of prayer and of support for service. Paul speaks to him with affection, as a spiritual father who encourages.

Paul writes from prison, near the end of his life. He remembers the sincere faith of Timothy's grandmother and mother. It seems Timothy was afraid or ashamed, so Paul encourages him not to draw back from ministry. Scholars debate exactly what the gift was, but it is connected to his service.

Today, do not let discouragement put out what God has given you. Set aside time to pray, to serve, and to use your gifts in your church or family, even when you feel fear.
exp.0:14:
Paul reminds Timothy that many in the province of Asia turned away from him. "They have turned against me" means that they withdrew from him or stopped supporting him. He names two of them: Phygellus and Hermogenes.

Paul writes from prison in Rome, near the end of his life, to encourage Timothy, his young co-worker. The texts do not explain in detail what those men did. Some think they were ashamed of Paul in his imprisonment or did not stand by him at his trial, but that is an interpretation. The contrast comes right after with Onesiphorus, who did seek him out and comfort him.

For today: when someone abandons you for following Christ, do not sink into bitterness. Remain faithful, and be the one who stands with, visits, and encourages those who suffer or are alone.
exp.1:17:
Paul says that Hymenaeus and Philetus had strayed from the truth. "Strayed" means they had left the right path. They taught that the resurrection had already taken place, that it had already happened. With that idea they were overturning the faith of some people, shaking it and throwing it into confusion.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, from a difficult moment in his life. He wants Timothy to guard sound teaching in the church. When he speaks of the resurrection as already past, many understand that these teachers saw it only as something spiritual and present, without expecting the future bodily resurrection. The text gives no further detail, so we do not know exactly what they said.

Today, let us not accept any teaching just because it sounds spiritual. Let us compare what we hear with the Bible, and with humility and love help those who are confused.
exp.0:7:
Paul asks Timothy not to be ashamed of speaking about Jesus, nor of Paul being in prison for His sake. On the contrary, he invites Timothy to suffer alongside him for the good news, relying on the power that God gives. Hardship here means suffering or difficulty, and power means strength.

Paul writes from prison, near the end of his life, to Timothy, his young co-worker. Timothy seems to have been fearful or timid, so Paul encourages him to stir up the gift God gave him. He reminds him that God does not give a spirit of fear, but of strength, love, and self-control.

For today: when speaking about your faith makes you feel embarrassed or afraid, remember that you do not depend on your own courage, but on the power of God. Ask Him for strength, and take a simple step, such as praying aloud or sharing your testimony with someone.
exp.3:19:
Paul tells Timothy where two co-workers were left. Erastus stayed behind in Corinth, and Trophimus he left at Miletus because he was sick. "Left" means he was left behind in that city, not that he abandoned him without concern.

Paul writes from prison, near the end of his life, and gives news to Timothy, his disciple. Erastus appears in other passages as a companion of Paul, but we do not know more about why he stayed in Corinth. We also do not know with certainty when the events at Miletus happened. It is surprising that Paul, who healed others, left a sick friend behind; the Bible does not explain this.

Even faithful servants get sick, and they are not always healed right away. If you are sick, or you know someone who is, remember that this does not cancel their worth or their faith. Pray, stay close, and help with kindness.
exp.1:13:
Paul tells Timothy to remind the believers of something important: that they should not fight or argue over words. "Charging them before the Lord" means warning them with seriousness, as those who stand before God. "Strive" means to fight or dispute. "Subverting" means throwing into disorder or doing harm, and "hearers" are those who listen to such arguments.

Paul writes from a difficult situation, near the end of his life, to encourage Timothy to be faithful. Earlier he spoke of God's faithfulness even when we fail. Now he warns that quarrels about words do not build up, but confuse and wound the faith of others.

Today we can ask ourselves before we argue: does this help someone know Christ better, or does it only feed my pride? Defending the truth is good, but it is wise to do so with humility, avoiding pointless arguments that divide and discourage.
exp.0:6:
He says that God did not give us a spirit of fear or cowardice. Instead, he gave us a spirit of power, of love, and of a sound mind. "Power" is strength or courage to act. "Sound mind" is self-control, that is, balance and good judgment so as not to be carried away by panic or by impulses.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, from prison. He reminds him of the sincere faith he inherited from his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice, and he encourages him to stir up the gift of God. Timothy seemed tempted to feel timidity or shame about the gospel and the suffering it brought. Paul urges him not to be ashamed.

When fear holds you back from doing what is right, remember that God gives you what you need. Ask him for courage to speak or act, love to do it with kindness, and a sound mind to respond with calm.
exp.3:7:
Paul says that a "crown of righteousness" is already reserved for him. That crown is a reward, like the prize a winner received in a race. The Lord, who is the righteous judge, will give it to him on that day, that is, when Christ returns. The promise is not only for Paul but for all who love the coming of Jesus.

Paul writes from prison, near the end of his life, to his young co-worker Timothy. He knows his death is near and looks back with peace: he fought the good fight, finished the race, and kept the faith. His hope does not rest on himself but on the just judgment of Christ. Then he asks Timothy to come to him soon, since some have left him.

For today: live with your eyes on the coming of Christ. Love it truly, be faithful in small things, and do not lose heart when others fail you; the Lord sees and rewards.
exp.1:21:
He tells Timothy to flee from youthful lusts, that is, from the impulses and passions typical of youth. Instead, he should pursue four things: righteousness (living uprightly), faith, charity, and peace. And he should do so together with those who call on the Lord with a pure heart, that is, with sincerity.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, from a difficult time, to encourage him to serve with firmness. It comes from the image of a great house with vessels for honor: whoever cleanses himself from what defiles can be useful to the Lord. Then Paul warns against foolish disputes. Scholars debate exactly what those youthful lusts cover, but the text suggests passions and also impatience or quarrels.

For today: it is not enough to avoid what is wrong; fill your life with what is good. Seek sincere friendships in the faith, and this week choose one concrete act of love or peace, such as making up with someone.
exp.1:2:
He says that Timothy must endure hardships and suffering, just as a loyal soldier serves Jesus Christ. The phrase meaning "endure hardship" refers to bearing trials and difficulties; the word for "loyal" describes someone steady and trustworthy.

The apostle Paul writes this letter to Timothy, his young co-worker, from prison, when he already sensed the end of his life drawing near. He has just asked Timothy to be strengthened by the grace of Christ and to pass the teaching on to trustworthy people. Then he uses the image of the soldier, who lives with one purpose: to please the one who enlisted him.

For today: serving Christ can bring discomfort, weariness, or rejection. Instead of being discouraged, remember that you are not alone, for strength comes from his grace. Today, persevere in a good task you have wanted to give up, and ask God for help to keep going faithfully.
exp.0:13:
He says that Timothy must carefully guard the good deposit, that is, something of great value that was entrusted to him. Here it refers to the message of the gospel and true teaching. He will not do this alone: he has the Holy Ghost, who dwells in believers. To keep means to protect and remain faithful.

The apostle Paul speaks, writing from prison to his young fellow worker Timothy. Paul suffers for the gospel, but he is not ashamed. He asks Timothy to hold firmly to the sound words he has learned, even though many in Asia had turned away from Paul.

Today we can guard what God has entrusted to us: the faith, the Word, and the truth. Reading the Bible with consistency, staying faithful when pressure comes, and asking the Holy Ghost for help each day helps us not to let go of what matters most.
exp.3:13:
Paul says that Alexander, a coppersmith (someone who works with copper or metals), did him much evil. He then adds: "the Lord reward him according to his works," that is, may God give him what his deeds deserve. The word "evil" refers to real harm, not mere annoyance.

Paul writes to Timothy from prison, near the end of his life. We do not know for certain what Alexander did; some think he accused Paul or opposed him during his trial, but the text does not give details. Paul warns Timothy to be on guard against him, because he opposed the message.

For today: when someone harms you, do not seek revenge. Leave the matter in God's hands, for he judges with justice, and be wise in protecting yourself. Paul, moreover, asked that forgiveness be granted to those who abandoned him (v. 16).
exp.0:11:
Paul says he suffers for preaching the gospel, but he feels no shame. The reason is that he knows Jesus personally, the one in whom he has trusted, and he is confident that Jesus is able to keep safe what Paul has entrusted to him until the day of Christ's return and the final judgment. "Suffer" means to endure hardship, and "what I have entrusted" can be understood as his life and salvation, or as the gospel that was committed to him; scholars interpret it in both ways.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, from prison, near the end of his life. He encourages him not to be ashamed of the gospel or of his imprisonment. His example shows steadfastness in the midst of pain.

For today: when faith costs you mockery, fear, or difficulties, do not rely only on your own strength. Know Christ better through prayer and Bible reading, and entrust to him with confidence whatever worries you most.
exp.2:8:
They say the false teachers will not succeed. Even though for a while they may seem to prosper, their folly, that is, their lack of wisdom and their foolishness, will be plain for everyone to see. Their folly will be as clear and evident as it was with Jannes and Jambres, names that Jewish tradition gives to the magicians who opposed Moses in Egypt (the Bible does not name them in the Old Testament).

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, from prison, near the end of his life. He warns him about people who look religious but are corrupt inside, and who resist the truth. He wants to encourage Timothy not to lose heart in the face of them.

For today: do not be anxious when error seems to be gaining ground. Stay firm in the truth, live with integrity, and trust that God, in his own time, makes clear what is false.
exp.3:16:
He says that, when everyone abandoned him, the Lord stood with Paul, gave him strength, and used him so that the message of the gospel would be fully proclaimed and heard by all the nations. "Gentiles" are the peoples who were not Jews.

Paul writes from prison, near the end of his life, to his young co-worker Timothy. At his first defense before the authorities, no one stood by him.

"Out of the mouth of the lion" is a figurative expression; it is not known with certainty whether it refers to a specific deadly danger, to an authority, or to the enemy in general, and it is interpreted in several ways.

For today: when you feel alone in your faith or in your responsibilities, remember that God does not leave you. Ask Him for strength and keep faithfully doing what He has entrusted to you, even when no one accompanies you.
exp.3:11:
It says that Paul sent Tychicus to the city of Ephesus. The word "sent" shows that Paul dispatched him with a task, and the name of the city is the form of Ephesus, an important city in Asia Minor.

Paul writes to Timothy from prison, near the end of his life. He is almost alone: Demas has left, others are on different missions, and only Luke remains with him. Tychicus appears in other letters as a faithful co-worker. It is not stated with certainty why he was sent; some think it may have been to take Timothy's place in Ephesus while Timothy traveled to Paul, but the text does not make this clear.

For today: serving God sometimes means going where help is needed, even when the role is not a visible one. Paul trusted Tychicus, and God values those who faithfully carry out what they are given to do.
exp.0:17:
He says that Paul wishes the Lord would grant Onesiphorus to find mercy from the Lord on that day, that is, the day of final judgment when Christ returns. He also recalls how much Onesiphorus helped him in Ephesus, something Timothy knew very well. The phrase "to find" in the verse means finding or receiving the mercy of the Lord.

Paul writes this letter from a prison in Rome, near the end of his life, to encourage his young co-worker Timothy. Onesiphorus was not ashamed that Paul was a prisoner; he searched for him with effort until he found him. Paul gives thanks by praying for him and for his household. Ephesus was the city where Timothy was serving, and there Onesiphorus had already helped. We do not know precisely what he did there.

Today we can imitate Onesiphorus: approaching with kindness those who suffer or are rejected for their faith, without shame. We can also pray for those who have blessed us, asking that God care for them with his mercy.
exp.1:0:
Paul says to Timothy, whom he calls "my son," that he should be strong, that is, that he should be made strong and take courage. But that strength does not come from himself, but from the grace that is in Christ Jesus: the favor and help of God that is received by being united to Jesus.

Paul writes this letter from prison, near the end of his life, according to Christian tradition. Timothy was his young co-worker and seemed to need encouragement in the face of difficulties and opposition. That is why Paul encourages him and asks him to faithfully pass on what he has learned to others, and to endure suffering like a good soldier.

For today: when you feel tired or afraid to keep going, do not rely only on your willpower. Pray each day asking for the grace of Christ, and take one concrete step of obedience today, trusting that He sustains you.
exp.1:1:
He says that Timothy should entrust and hand on the teachings he heard from Paul, in front of many witnesses, to faithful and trustworthy people. The words "to entrust" are rendered in the verse above as "commit," meaning to hand over something valuable to someone's care. The phrase "able to teach" describes people who are capable and qualified to do so. These people, in turn, will teach others.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, from prison, near the end of his life. He wants to make sure the gospel keeps going after him. He speaks of four generations: Paul, Timothy, the faithful men, and others. The "many witnesses" may have been people present when Paul taught or entrusted Timothy with these things, though some scholars understand this in different ways.

Think of someone you can teach what you have learned about Christ: a child, a friend, or a new believer. Choose someone faithful, spend time walking alongside them, and encourage them to pass it on to others afterward.
exp.2:13:
It says Timothy should keep firm in what he has already learned and in what he came to believe with conviction. Also, Paul reminds him to think about the people who taught him, that is, people he could trust.

Paul writes this letter to Timothy, his young co-worker, while he is in prison and near the end of his life. He has just warned him that there will be persecution and that deceivers will go from bad to worse. That is why he encourages him not to be carried away by false teachings. The verses that follow mention the Scriptures Timothy had known since childhood. Many understand that this also refers to his grandmother and mother, although this verse does not name them.

When there is confusion or pressure, go back to what you have learned from the Bible, and remember the people who taught it to you by their lives and their words.
exp.2:0:
He says that Timothy must know something important: that in the "last days", that is, in the final times, "perilous" periods will come. The old word "last" means "final", and "perilous" refers to times that are hard and difficult to endure, not merely risky.

Paul writes this letter to Timothy, his young co-worker, from prison, near the end of his life. He wants to prepare him to serve with steadfastness. Some believe the "last days" are the time between the first and second coming of Christ; others think of a final period. The verses that follow describe what people will be like, and that shows that the danger comes above all from the human heart.

For today: do not be amazed if the world becomes selfish and hard. Ask God to guard you from that spirit, and seek to live with humility, love, and faithfulness to Jesus.
exp.0:9:
It says that the grace God planned from before time has now been made visible through the coming of Jesus Christ. He has abolished death, meaning he took away its final power, and through the gospel he has brought life and immortality into the light, that is, he made them clear and known. The word for his coming here means his arrival into this world.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, from prison and near the end of his life. He wants to encourage him not to be ashamed of the gospel or of Paul being in chains, and to suffer for it with the strength God gives. Paul bases that encouragement on what Christ has already done.

For today: if Christ has overcome death, we can face fear, loss, and mockery with hope. Today you can speak about your faith simply, without shame, trusting that God sustains his people.
exp.3:20:
Paul asks Timothy to do everything he can to come before winter begins. Then he sends greetings from four people who are with him in Rome: Eubulus, Pudens, Linus, and Claudia, along with all the brothers and sisters.

Paul writes from prison, near the end of his life. He feels alone, since several co-workers have left, and he wants to see Timothy. In winter sea travel and journeys were difficult, which is why the urgency.

Beyond these names, the Bible says little about them, and we cannot know much more with certainty.

For today: do not put off visiting or keeping company with someone who needs you. A phone call, a visit, or a timely message can be a great comfort, and a united church shows itself in these small details of care.
exp.2:11:
It says that all who want to live a godly life, that is, honoring God in the way they live, united with Christ Jesus, will suffer persecution. "Godly" means with reverence and devotion to God. "Will suffer" means they will endure or bear it.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, from a difficult time, when he was in prison. He reminds him of what he himself suffered in Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra, and that the Lord delivered him. Then he warns that evil people will go from bad to worse, and he asks Timothy to remain steadfast in what he has learned.

For today: if you face mockery or rejection for living with integrity and faith, do not think that God has abandoned you. Stay firm, pray, and seek the support of brothers and sisters in the faith.
exp.3:5:
Paul says he is already ready to be "offered," that is, poured out as an offering to God. That word recalls the drink offerings of wine that were poured out over a sacrifice. And "departure" means his leaving of this life, his death, which is now drawing near.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, from prison, probably shortly before his death. He has just warned him that many will abandon the truth for myths, and he asks him to remain faithful. Now Paul shows him by his own example how a life given to Christ ends: with peace and hope, not with fear.

Live today in such a way that your life is an offering to God, not only at the end. Be faithful in the small things of each day, trusting that God keeps what you have entrusted to Him.
exp.0:3:
Paul says he has a strong desire to see Timothy. He remembers Timothy's tears and thinks that seeing him again would make his joy complete.

Paul writes this letter from prison, near the end of his life, to Timothy, whom he regards as a son in the faith. The text does not say for certain when Timothy wept. Some think it was at a farewell, but the Bible does not make this clear. What is clear is a deep and sincere affection.

For today: do not keep your affection for your brothers and sisters in the faith to yourself. Write to or call someone today who has been important in your Christian life, tell them you remember them, and pray for that person. A simple gesture can bring a great deal of encouragement.
exp.0:2:
Paul thanks God, whom he serves as his forefathers did, and he does so with a clear conscience. He says that he never stops remembering Timothy in his prayers, night and day. The phrase "without ceasing" means constantly, never letting time pass without praying for him.

Paul writes this letter to Timothy, his son in the faith, from prison, near the end of his life. He wants to encourage him to remain steadfast in service. Before giving advice, he shows affection and tells him that he holds him in mind before God. Scholars agree that this is a very personal letter.

Praying regularly for the people God has placed in your life is a great gift. Choose someone today, perhaps a younger believer, a family member, or a friend, and pray for him by name. Then, if you can, let him know that you remember him.
exp.3:10:
It says that Luke is the only one still at Paul's side. Paul asks Timothy to bring Mark, because Mark is profitable to him for the ministry, meaning useful and of good service.

Paul writes from prison, near the end of his life. Other co-workers had left: Demas, because he loved this world, and others for different tasks. Mark is probably John Mark, with whom Paul had a disagreement years earlier (Acts 15:37-39). Now Paul values him and asks for him, which suggests a restored relationship.

For today: do not write anyone off for good. If someone failed and has since grown, give them a new opportunity. And if you have failed, keep serving faithfully: God can make you useful again.
exp.3:14:
Paul tells Timothy to be on his guard against Alexander the coppersmith. "Be on your guard" means take care, be alert. "Greatly" means very much. Alexander strongly opposed the teaching of Paul and his companions.

Paul writes from prison, near the end of his life, to his young co-worker Timothy. He had already mentioned the harm Alexander did to him, but he does not leave revenge in his own hands: he asks that the Lord be the one to judge. Here he gives Timothy a practical warning. The Bible does not say in detail what Alexander did, so it is best not to imagine more than what is written.

We can be wise with those who oppose the gospel or harm others, without repaying evil with evil. Taking care is not the same as hating. One can set sensible limits and, at the same time, leave justice in God's hands.
exp.3:8:
It says that Timothy should do everything he can to get to where Paul is quickly. "Make every effort" means try hard, do whatever is within your power. "Shortly" is an old word meaning soon or quickly. "Unto me" is simply "to me."

The apostle Paul speaks here, writing to his young coworker Timothy. According to the letter, Paul is in prison and feels that his life is nearing its end. He has just said that he has fought the good fight. Now he shows his human side: some have left him, and he needs company. He says that only Luke is with him. How much time Timothy had to arrive we do not know for certain.

All of us need company, even those who are strongest in faith. Today you might think of someone who is alone, sick, or tired, and not wait for another day: call them, visit them, or write to them. Sometimes your presence is worth more than a thousand words.
exp.1:8:
Paul says that because of the gospel he suffers hardship and is even chained, as if he were a criminal. But he makes something very important clear: even though he is tied up, the word of God is not imprisoned. In other words, no one can chain it or stop it.

Paul is writing to Timothy, his young co-worker, from a situation of imprisonment, and Christian tradition places him in Rome toward the end of his life. He wants to encourage Timothy not to be ashamed of the gospel and to remain firm, even when it costs him. Paul himself is the example: he suffers, but he does so out of love for the chosen, so that others may come to know Christ.

Today, when we face trials, limits, or criticism for following Jesus, let us remember that our circumstances do not stop God. We can keep sharing his word with love and trust, even in difficult times.
exp.3:17:
Paul says that the Lord will rescue him from every evil and keep him safe until he enters his heavenly kingdom. "Will keep" means to care for and keep safe. "Evil work" refers to any attack or wickedness that seeks to turn him away from the faith. He ends by praising God: "to whom be glory forever."

Paul writes this letter to Timothy from prison, near the end of his life. He has just said that his friends abandoned him at his first hearing, but that the Lord stood by his side. Many understand "the lion's mouth" as an expression of extreme danger; it is not known with certainty whether it refers to something literal. His confidence is not in escaping death, but in God sustaining him to the end.

When you feel alone or pressured, remember that God does not let go of you. He may not remove every difficulty, but he can sustain you and keep you in the faith. Today, bring to God in prayer whatever worries you, and thank him for his care.
exp.2:3:
It says that in the last times there will be people who are disloyal (traitors), impulsive and without self-control (headstrong), and full of pride (puffed up, as if inflated with themselves). Above all, it describes people who love pleasure more than they love God. It does not say that pleasure is bad in itself, but that it takes the place that belongs to God.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, from prison, near the end of his life. He wants to prepare him for difficult times in the church. The verses that follow say that some will have the appearance of godliness but without living its power, so Paul advises Timothy to stay away from them.

For today: ask yourself honestly what holds first place in your heart. Enjoying what is good is a gift from God, but ask Him to remain your greatest love.
exp.2:15:
This verse says that all of Scripture comes from God. "Given by inspiration" means that God himself breathed it out, or gave it. That is why it is useful for teaching the truth, for showing where error lies and rebuking it, for correcting, which means helping a person get back on the right path, and for training in righteousness, which means shaping a person toward an upright life.

Paul is writing to Timothy, his young co-worker, near the end of his life. He asks him to remain firm in what he has learned since childhood, since the Scriptures lead to salvation through faith in Christ. The verses that follow say that in this way the believer is prepared for every good work. When Paul speaks of "all Scripture," he had in mind the Hebrew Scriptures, and Christians have understood the principle to apply to the whole Bible.

For today: read the Bible not only to gain information, but also letting it teach you and correct you. Ask yourself each day: "What does God want to change in me through this passage?"
exp.1:3:
It says that a soldier on active duty does not get tangled up in the "affairs of this life," that is, in the ordinary matters and daily routines, because he wants to please the one who enlisted him. The verse of the word "entangleth" is that it means "gets caught up" or "lets himself be bound." The verse of the word "soldier" is that it means "serves as a soldier."

Paul writes to Timothy from prison, near the end of his life. He wants to encourage his young co-worker to teach faithfully and to endure suffering for the gospel. He uses the image of the soldier, along with those of the athlete and the farmer. Paul does not say that working or having a family is wrong, but that nothing should get in the way of loyalty to Christ.

Today we might ask ourselves which matters, even good ones, are tangling us up and taking our focus off serving Christ. Setting clear priorities, and perhaps saying "no" to some things, helps us live to please him.
exp.2:12:
This verse says that evil people and those who deceive others will not get better over time, but will keep getting worse. Their deception has two sides: they deceive others, and at the same time they themselves end up deceived.

Paul writes to Timothy from prison, near the end of his life. He has just reminded him of the persecutions Paul suffered and how the Lord delivered him. Now he warns him that there will be people who move further and further away from the truth. With this, he prepares Timothy so that he will not lose heart and will remain firm in what he has learned.

For today: do not be surprised or discouraged when deception seems to be spreading. Stay close to the Bible, and before following any teaching or popular voice, compare it with what the Scriptures say.
exp.3:15:
Paul tells us that, when he first defended himself before the court, no one stood by him to support him. All of them abandoned him. "Forsook" means leaving someone alone, and "laid to their charge" means not holding it against them as a fault. Paul hopes that God will not hold that failure against them.

Paul writes to Timothy from prison, near the end of his life. He has just spoken about Alexander, who did him a great deal of harm. Even so, Paul does not dwell on the complaint: he says that the Lord stood with him and gave him strength to proclaim the gospel. Interpreters do not agree on exactly what that "first answer" was.

For today: when someone fails you in a difficult moment, you can be honest about your pain and still forgive. Ask the Lord to sustain you, and trust that He will not leave you alone.
exp.0:15:
Here Paul asks that the Lord show mercy to the household of Onesiphorus. He says that Onesiphorus often refreshed him, that is, he encouraged him, comforted him, and gave him relief. And that he was not ashamed of his chain, that is, of the fact that Paul was in prison.

Paul writes to Timothy from prison, near the end of his life. He has just mentioned that many in Asia turned away from him. By contrast, he highlights Onesiphorus, who searched diligently for him in Rome until he found him. His household is mentioned, which suggests that his family also took part, though the text gives no further details.

Today, we can imitate Onesiphorus: approaching without shame someone who suffers, whether sick, imprisoned, or abandoned. A visit, a phone call, or a concrete act of help can be a true rest from God for that person.
exp.1:22:
It says we should reject foolish and senseless arguments. The words that the verse uses for "foolish and unlearned" are the ones on the page, and "questions" means debates or disputes; "avoid" means to set aside or turn away from; and "gender" means to produce or give rise to. In other words, those arguments do not build anyone up; they only produce quarrels.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, near the end of his life. He asks him to be a clean and useful vessel for God. Shortly before, he spoke of people who get lost in arguments about words. Then he explains that the servant of the Lord must be gentle and patient, so as to correct with humility.

For today: before entering a debate, ask yourself whether it will help someone come to know the truth or will only feed pride and anger. If it is only going to produce a fight, as on social media or within the family, it is better to keep silent, pray, and respond with calm and kindness.
exp.3:6:
Paul says that he has fought the good fight, that he has reached the finish of his race, and that he has been faithful to what God entrusted to him. "Keeping the faith" can be understood as remaining loyal to Christ and guarding the message of the gospel without changing it. The images of fighting and of running a race are drawn from struggle and athletics.

Paul writes from prison, near the end of his life. He knows that his departure, that is, his death, is near. He speaks to Timothy, his young co-worker, to encourage him to remain steadfast in ministry. After saying this, Paul speaks of the crown of righteousness that the Lord will give to all who love his appearing.

For today: this is not about being perfect, but about being faithful to the end. Today you can choose one concrete decision of obedience to God, even a small one, and remain steadfast in it with perseverance.
exp.3:21:
Paul closes with a blessing. First he wishes Timothy that the Lord Jesus Christ be with his spirit, that is, with him in the innermost part of his being. Then he says "Grace be with you," which in the verse your reader sees is "Grace be with you": here he speaks to the whole church, not only to Timothy. The final note about Timothy, Ephesus, Rome and Nero is not part of the original text; it was added later by copyists, and scholars doubt its accuracy.

Paul writes from prison, near the end of his life, to his young co-worker Timothy. He asks him to come soon and sends greetings from friends. He closes with a prayer, because he knows Timothy will need the strength of God to keep going in the ministry.

Today we can say goodbye to others with a sincere blessing, not only with a "goodbye." This week, pray for someone and ask God that his grace and presence go with them in whatever they are facing.
exp.1:12:
It says that even if we fail or are not faithful, Christ remains faithful. The phrase "if we become unfaithful" or "if we fail to trust" is not used here, so I will simply say it means that even if we become unfaithful, he stays faithful. The phrase "deny himself" means acting against what he is. Christ cannot stop being faithful, because that is his character.

Paul writes to Timothy from prison, near the end of his life. He has just quoted what seems to be a Christian hymn or saying about dying, suffering, and reigning with Christ, and about the consequences of denying him. Some understand this verse as comfort for the believer who stumbles; others, as a warning that God also carries out his judgments. Both readings are debated.

For today: if you have failed, do not hide from God. Return to him with humility, trusting that his faithfulness does not depend on yours, and ask him for the strength to keep going.
exp.3:1:
What it says: Paul charges Timothy to proclaim God's message and to be persistent, whether the moment is convenient or inconvenient. Paul's words "in season and out of season" describe this. "Reprove" means to show the error clearly; "rebuke" means to correct; "exhort" means to encourage. Everything must be done with great patience and good teaching.

Context: Paul writes from prison, near the end of his life, to Timothy, his young co-worker. He solemnly charges him before God and Christ Jesus, who will judge everyone. The following verses explain the urgency: a time will come when many will not want to hear sound teaching and will look for teachers who tell them what they like.

For today: If you need to correct or advise someone, do it with the Bible, with love and with patience, not with anger or only to win an argument. And examine whether you yourself are willing to hear the truth, even when it is uncomfortable.
exp.3:12:
Paul asks Timothy to bring with him, when he comes, the cloak (a heavy coat for the cold) that he left at Troas, at the house of a man named Carpus. He also asks for the books, and especially the parchments, which were rolls made of animal skin and probably contained important writings.

Paul writes from prison, near the end of his life. He is almost alone, since Luke is the only one who is with him. It is not known for certain what the books and parchments contained; some think they were texts of the Scriptures, but this is a supposition.

God takes care of our needs of body and soul. Paul, even though he was an apostle, needed warmth and study. Do not be ashamed to ask for practical help, and keep feeding your mind and your faith through reading.
exp.3:3:
This verse says that some people will stop listening to the truth and will turn toward fables, that is, invented stories, myths, or ideas that sound appealing but are not true. In the verse as it reads in your Bible, "turn away their ears" means refusing to hear, and "turned unto" means being diverted toward something else.

Paul writes to Timothy from prison, near the end of his life. He knows his death is approaching and charges Timothy to preach the Word with firmness. He warns that there will be people who cannot endure sound teaching and will seek out teachers who tell them what they want to hear.

For today: before accepting a teaching, compare it with what the Bible says. Ask yourself honestly whether you are seeking the truth or only what makes you feel comfortable, and let the Word correct you.
exp.0:16:
It says that Onesiphorus, when he arrived in Rome, sought out Paul with great care and effort until he found him. The words "very diligently" mean searching with energy, putting in effort and attention. The phrase "and found me" indicates that it was not easy, but he did not give up.

Paul writes to Timothy from prison, near the end of his life. Many in Asia had turned away from him. By contrast, Onesiphorus was not ashamed that Paul was imprisoned. Paul remembers him with gratitude and asks the Lord for mercy for his household. We do not know with certainty all the details of that search.

Today, we can imitate Onesiphorus by intentionally seeking out those who suffer, who are alone, or who are going through trials. A visit, a phone call, or a concrete act of help can be a great comfort, even when it costs time or discomfort.
exp.3:18:
Paul asks Timothy to pass on his greetings to three friends: Prisca (or Priscilla), her husband Aquila, and the entire household of Onesiphorus.

Paul writes this letter from prison, near the end of his life, and Timothy is in Ephesus. Prisca and Aquila had been faithful co-workers of Paul for many years. About Onesiphorus, 2 Timothy 1:16-18 says that Paul was encouraged by him and was not ashamed of his chains. Even at a solemn moment, Paul warmly remembers those who stood with him.

For today: do not underestimate small gestures. A greeting, a phone call, or a prayer for those who have supported you in hard times can be a great encouragement. Today, think of someone who has helped you in your faith and thank them.
exp.1:19:
This verse compares the church to a great house. In such a house there are dishes and vessels made of different materials: vessels of gold and silver, and also of wood and clay. Some serve noble purposes, "to honour," and others serve common or humble uses, "to dishonour."

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, from prison, toward the end of his life. He has just mentioned false teachers, such as Hymenaeus and Philetus, who taught errors and harmed the faith of others. Interpreters debate whether the "great house" means the church in general or something broader, but the following verse makes the message clear: each person can choose to cleanse himself from evil.

For today: examine what in your life pulls you away from God, such as bad company, habits, or false teachings, and turn away from them with his help. In this way you can be useful to him.
exp.0:12:
Paul tells Timothy to hold on to the pattern of "sound words," that is, the true and wholesome teaching he received from him. "Hold fast" means to keep firmly to something, and "form" refers to a pattern or outline that serves as a guide. That teaching is to be lived out in the faith and love found in Christ Jesus.

Paul writes from prison, near the end of his life, to his young co-worker Timothy. He suffers for preaching the gospel, but he is not ashamed, because he trusts in God. Many have turned away from him, and Paul wants Timothy not to lose heart or change the message.

For today: it is not enough to know correct doctrine; it must be held with love. When you teach or talk about your faith, seek to be faithful to the Bible and, at the same time, to treat others with patience and kindness.
exp.2:2:
He says that in the last times there will be people "without natural affection," that is, without natural love, not even for their own family. "Trucebreakers" are those who do not keep their word or who refuse to forgive. "False accusers" speak badly of others with lies. "Incontinent" means without self-control, letting themselves be carried away by their impulses. "Fierce" describes those who are harsh and without compassion. "Despisers of those that are good" are those who reject what is good.

The apostle Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, from a difficult moment in his life. He wants to prepare him to shepherd people in complicated times. He describes how those who live far from God behave, even when they appear to be religious. There are different opinions about exactly when "the last days" are fulfilled, but the counsel serves for any era.

Today we can examine our own treatment of others: Do I speak well of people, forgive, have patience and show affection? Let us ask God that his love change us from within.
exp.1:24:
This verse says that the servant of the Lord must correct with meekness, that is, with a kind and humble manner, those who oppose him. The words "if God peradventure" and "in meekness" are old-fashioned forms; today we would say "perhaps" and "gently." The idea is that God may perhaps grant them repentance, meaning a change in the way they think, so that they come to acknowledge the truth.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, who was caring for the church in an atmosphere of arguments and false teaching. Earlier he had asked him to avoid foolish debates that only produce quarrels. Here he shows him how to deal with opponents: without fighting, teaching with patience. The following verse speaks of people caught by the devil, and of their being able to escape that snare.

Today, when someone thinks differently from you, respond with calm and respect, without trying to win arguments by shouting. Remember that only God changes the heart; you can speak the truth with kindness and pray for that person.
exp.2:1:
This verse begins a list of attitudes that Paul describes in people of the "last days." It says there will be people centered on themselves, who love money, who boast, who are proud, and who speak evil of others. They will also be rebellious toward their parents, ungrateful, and unholy, that is, without a desire to live set apart for God.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, from a difficult time, probably when he was in prison. He wants to prepare him to shepherd the church in the midst of wickedness. The "last days" are understood as the time from Christ until his return, and some believers also see it as a future stage.

Today, examine your heart with this list. Ask God to help you be more thankful, honor your family, and serve others without seeking your own recognition.
exp.1:25:
The verse says that people who oppose the truth can "recover themselves" (get loose, be freed) from a devil's trap. That trap is like a snare, a rope that catches an animal. They are "taken captive," that is, held, trapped, under the enemy's control. The hope is that, by repenting, they will be set free.

Paul writes to Timothy, a young pastor, near the end of his life. He advises him on how to treat those who argue and oppose the teaching. Some scholars debate whether "at his will" refers to the devil or to God; both readings are possible.

Today, when someone thinks differently from you or is caught in an error, do not win the argument with harshness. Respond with patience and kindness, and pray that God opens their eyes. Remember that it was God who also set you free.
exp.3:2:
It says that a time will come when people will not put up with sound teaching, that is, the teaching that is correct and healthy. Because they have "itching ears," meaning a desire to hear only what pleases them, they will surround themselves with teachers who tell them what their own desires want to hear.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, from prison, near the end of his life. He has just asked him to preach the Word with patience, even when it is not comfortable or popular. He warns that there will be people who reject that truth.

For today: examine with humility what kind of teaching you seek. Do not surround yourself only with voices that agree with you; compare what you hear with the Bible, and let it correct you too.
exp.3:4:
Unlike those who seek teachings that suit their own tastes, Timothy is told to stay alert in every situation. To be watchful means to stay awake and attentive. To endure afflictions means to bear suffering without giving up. Doing the work of an evangelist means proclaiming the good news of Jesus. Making full proof of your ministry means carrying out completely the service God entrusted to you.

Paul writes from prison, knowing that his death is near. He speaks to Timothy, his young co-worker, who would be left to guide the church. Earlier, he warns that people will come who prefer teachers who tell them what they want to hear. For this reason, Paul encourages him to be firm and faithful, as Paul himself was.

For today: do not let yourself be carried along by what is fashionable or by what is comfortable. Ask God for firmness to follow his Word, even when it costs you, and serve with steadiness in what he has entrusted to you.
exp.1:6:
Paul asks Timothy to think carefully about what he has just told him. Paul's word for this is reflect and meditate, not merely listen. Then Paul prays that the Lord will give him understanding, that is, the ability to grasp and apply everything.

Paul writes from prison to Timothy, his young co-worker. He has just used three examples: the soldier, the athlete who competes according to the rules, and the farmer. All of them speak of discipline, rules, and steady effort. Paul does not explain each comparison, so he invites Timothy to discover their meaning, trusting in God's help.

For today: do not settle for a quick reading of the Bible. Take a few minutes to think about what it teaches you, and ask God to give you understanding, because reflection and prayer belong together.
exp.2:7:
It says that, just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, there are also people who oppose the truth of the gospel. The phrase about being rejected in the faith means those who are worthless when it comes to faith: they do not pass the test. The phrase about corrupt minds speaks of a damaged mind, twisted by its own desires.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, from prison, near the end of his life. The names Jannes and Jambres do not appear in the Old Testament; Jewish tradition identifies them with the magicians of Egypt who confronted Moses. Paul warns Timothy about false teachers, but he assures him that they will not prevail.

For today: do not become discouraged when you see the truth rejected or twisted teachings spreading. Hold firmly to the Word, examine what you hear with humility, and trust that God will make clear what is false.
exp.0:4:
Paul says that he remembers the sincere faith of Timothy. The faith is genuine, without any pretense or hypocrisy. That faith first lived in his grandmother Lois and in his mother Eunice, and Paul is sure that it also lives in Timothy.

Paul writes this letter to Timothy, his young co-worker, probably from prison and near the end of his life. He encourages him because Timothy seems discouraged or fearful. Before asking him to stir up the gift of God, Paul reminds him of his history of faith and how much he loves him.

For today: thank those who taught you to believe, perhaps a grandmother, a mother, or another person. If you influence children or young people, be steady and sincere in your faith, because your example can sustain them for a long time.
exp.0:10:
This verse says that Paul was appointed, that is, named or designated, for three tasks: preacher (the one who announces the message), apostle (sent with authority by Christ), and teacher of the Gentiles, that is, of the peoples who were not Jews. With "of which" he refers to the gospel mentioned earlier.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, from prison, near the end of his life. He wants to encourage him not to be afraid or ashamed of the gospel. Paul reminds him that his own calling did not come from himself but from God, and that he is suffering because of this message.

For today: God also entrusts you with something, even if you are not a preacher. You can speak about Jesus with your words and your example in your family or at work. If it is hard for you or makes you feel embarrassed, remember that God is the one who sustains you.
exp.2:14:
He says that Timothy has known the Holy Scriptures since childhood. Those Scriptures, that is, what we today call the Old Testament, can give him wisdom for "salud," which here means salvation. That salvation comes through faith in Christ Jesus. The Bible does not save by itself; it points to Christ, and faith in Him is what saves.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young coworker, from a difficult time, near the end of his life. He has just warned him about deceiving men. For that reason he asks him to stay firm in what he has learned. According to 2 Timothy 1:5, his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice passed on the faith to him, though the text gives no further details about how they taught him.

For today: spend a few minutes each day reading the Bible looking for Christ in it. If you have children or nephews and nieces, read to them with affection; that seed can stay with them their whole life.
exp.2:6:
This verse speaks of people who are always learning but never come to know the truth. The phrase "never able to come to the knowledge of the truth" in your verse is the wording this comment is about, and "to come to" here means to reach it fully. In other words, they listen, study, and gather information, but they never settle into what is true.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, from prison, near the end of his life. He warns about people with a religious appearance who take advantage of vulnerable people in their homes. Paul does not condemn learning itself, but an aimless curiosity without obedience, one that also resists the truth, as Jannes and Jambres did. Those names come from Jewish tradition and do not appear in the Old Testament.

For today: accumulating teachings, videos, or debates is not enough. Ask yourself: "What truth that I already know am I willing to obey?" Knowing the truth includes humility and putting it into practice.
exp.1:15:
He tells Timothy to turn away from empty talk that offends God. "Profane" words are those that have nothing sacred about them. "Vain babblings" are chatter without value or benefit. "Ungodliness" means living without reverence for God. The verse warns that those who get caught up in such talk move further and further away from God.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, from prison, near the end of his life. He wants Timothy to guard sound teaching in the church. Shortly after, he gives examples: Hymenaeus and Philetus, who taught that the resurrection had already happened and upset the faith of some.

Today we might ask ourselves which arguments, gossip or debates wear us down without building anyone up. It is wise to step away from them and devote that time to knowing the Bible, so that we speak with truth and with love.
exp.1:4:
This verse says that someone who takes part in a competition does not receive the victor's crown if they do not compete according to the rules. Here "strive" means to compete or contend, like an athlete in the games. "Lawfully" means in accordance with the established rules. "Crowned" refers to the winner's prize.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, from a difficult moment in his life, and encourages him to remain steadfast in the ministry. He uses three examples: the soldier, the athlete, and the farmer. All of them speak of discipline, effort, and perseverance. Some understand the rules to refer to serving God with integrity and faithfulness to the apostolic teaching.

For today: it is not enough to want good results; how we seek them matters. Serve God, work, and study with honesty, without shortcuts or tricks, trusting that he is the one who gives the prize.
exp.2:16:
This verse says that Scripture has a purpose: that the person who serves God be complete and well prepared. "Perfect" here means mature and fully equipped, not someone without any flaw. "Thoroughly furnished" means well trained, and "good works" refers to any action that pleases God and helps others.

The apostle Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, near the end of his life. He encourages him to stand firm in what he learned since childhood, in the midst of false teachings and difficulties. Paul shows that the Bible, inspired by God, teaches, corrects, and shapes character, and so prepares the believer to serve.

For today: read the Bible regularly, not only to know more, but to obey. Ask yourself each day: "What good work is God asking me to do with what I have just read?"
exp.1:5:
This verse says that the farmer, if he wants to receive the fruits of his harvest, must first work. The phrase "must be" in the verse expresses this necessity. Effort comes first, and the reward comes afterward.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, from a difficult moment in his life, and encourages him to be faithful in the ministry. He uses three examples in a row: the soldier, the athlete, and the farmer. All of them speak of dedication, discipline, and perseverance. Some scholars understand that the fruit also refers to sharing in the benefits of the work, but the general sense is clear: serving God requires patient effort.

For today: do not become discouraged if you do not see results soon. Keep being faithful in your work, your family, your church, and your life with God, trusting that steady effort, done with love, will bear its fruit in due time.

sum.1: Paul encourages Timothy to be strong in the grace of Christ, to teach other faithful people, and to endure suffering like a good soldier, remembering that Christ rose from the dead and that God remains faithful. He also asks Timothy to teach the Word well, avoid foolish arguments, flee from evil desires, and correct others with gentleness.
sum.0: Paul, imprisoned for the gospel, encourages his dear son Timothy to stir up the gift of God, not to be afraid or ashamed of Christ, and to remain steadfast in the faith and the sound words. He reminds him that God saved us by his grace, not by our works. He also mentions those who abandoned him and Onesiphorus, who helped him.
sum.2: Paul warns Timothy that in the last days there will be difficult times, with people who are selfish and proud and who appear to be godly, and he tells Timothy to stay away from them. He reminds him of his own example of faith and suffering, and says that those who live for Christ will be persecuted. He encourages Timothy to remain firm in the Scriptures, which are inspired by God and prepare us for every good work.
sum.3: Paul charges Timothy to preach the word with patience, even though a time is coming when people will prefer teachers who tell them what they want to hear. Knowing that his death is near, Paul says he has fought the good fight and looks forward to the crown the Lord will give. He asks Timothy to come to him soon, because nearly everyone has left him, but the Lord has strengthened him.
